prompt.context: Our client is a private equity firm that has just purchased a motorcycle manufacturer based in Germany that makes sporty bikes. Currently they supply motorcycles to Europe but have no presence in the US. They are looking to expand the business into the US but are unsure of how to do this. They are considering two models: one is selling through existing dealerships in the US, the other is building a flagship dealership and selling that way.
prompt.question: Our client wants to consider a few issues. First, is this expansion a good idea? Second, which model would be the best to pursue? As a starting point, tell me a little about the high level pros and cons of building a flagship dealership versus selling through existing channels.

clarifying_info.q: What is the retail price of the motorcycle?
What does the motorcycle cost to produce?
clarifying_info.a: Cost to produce is $10K per bike.

clarifying_info.q: What is the cost to set up a flagship dealership?
clarifying_info.a: $3 million to set up a flagship store.

clarifying_info.q: What are the startup costs for the existing channel model?
What margin do distributors require in the existing channel model?
clarifying_info.a: Distributors require 33% gross margin on retail price, plus a 3% allowance on sales price reserved for returns and selling costs.

clarifying_info.q: What is the size of the US motorcycle market?
clarifying_info.a: 100K bikes are sold in the US every year. 15% are from Europe, 30% are high-end ($20K or higher), and roughly 10% are sporty.

exhibits.title: US Motorcycle Market Breakdown
exhibits.shows: A bar chart breaking down 100K annual US motorcycle unit sales across three dimensions: country of origin (Europe vs. Other), price (under $20K vs. $20K and over), and type (sporty vs. non-sporty).

framework: Assess strategic rationale for US expansion (market attractiveness, competitive landscape, PE client profile)
Evaluate two entry models: flagship dealership vs. existing distribution channels
Quantify profitability and breakeven for each model
Size the addressable market using exhibit data
Synthesize into a recommendation accounting for PE's desire for quick returns and low capital deployment

questions.prompt: What are the high-level pros and cons of building a flagship dealership versus selling through existing channels?
questions.guidance: Flagship pros: higher margins (own distribution), full control over brand positioning and sales training, ownership of customer data and marketing. Flagship cons: large capital investment ($3M), no existing customer relationships or local market knowledge, brand not yet known in the US. Existing channel pros: lower upfront capital ($250K), leverage existing relationships and local knowledge, faster ramp-up. Existing channel cons: lower margins (distributor takes 33% + 3% allowance), less brand control.

questions.prompt: Calculate the breakeven number of bikes for each model.
questions.guidance: Flagship: profit per bike = $20K - $10K = $10K. Breakeven = $3,000K / $10K = 300 bikes. Existing channel: distributor takes 33% of $20K = $6.6K, leaving $13.4K to client. 3% allowance on $20K = $0.6K, leaving net ~$13K per bike. Profit per bike = $13K - $10K = $3K. Breakeven = $250K / $3K ≈ 83 bikes.

math.setup: Flagship: Fixed cost = $3,000K; margin per bike = Retail - Cost = $20K - $10K = $10K. Existing: Fixed cost = $250K; distributor margin = 33% x $20K = $6.6K; 3% allowance = 3% x $20K = $0.6K; net revenue per bike = $20K - $6.6K - $0.6K = $12.8K ≈ $13K; margin per bike = $13K - $10K = $3K.
math.answer: Flagship breakeven: 300 bikes. Existing channel breakeven: ~83 bikes.

questions.prompt: Using the exhibit, size the addressable market and assess feasibility of the breakeven targets.
questions.guidance: 100K total US bikes sold per year. 15% European origin = 15K bikes. 30% high-end ($20K+) = 30K bikes. 10% sporty = 10K bikes. Narrowing by all three: 15% European x 30% high-end x 10% sporty = 15K x 30% = 4,500 x 10% = 450 bikes. At 450 bikes total addressable (European sporty high-end), 300 flagship breakeven is a stretch and 83 existing-channel breakeven may also be challenging with competitors. Note: interviewer may push back that country of origin is irrelevant; if so, addressable market = 30% x 10% x 100K = 3,000 bikes, making both breakevens more feasible.

math.setup: Total US market = 100K units. Apply three filters sequentially or combined.
steps: If origin irrelevant: high-end sporty = 30% x 10% x 100K = 3,000 bikes
math.answer: Narrow addressable market: ~450 bikes (European origin applied). Broad addressable market: ~3,000 bikes (origin irrelevant).

questions.prompt: Given that this is a PE client, what is your recommendation on the entry model?
questions.guidance: PE firms typically seek to flip investments quickly and minimize capital deployment. Flagship requires $3M upfront and a longer payback period; existing channels require only $250K and break even at just 83 bikes. Short-term the better play is existing distribution channels. The PE client may also want to explore whether growing in other European markets is more efficient before committing to the US. Long-term, a flagship is more profitable per bike but misaligned with typical PE holding periods.

recommendation: Use existing US distribution channels as the primary entry model given the PE client's preference for capital efficiency and quick returns
The existing channel model breaks even at only ~83 bikes vs. 300 for a flagship, requiring far less upfront capital ($250K vs. $3M)
If the addressable US market is ~3,000 high-end sporty bikes annually, both breakevens are achievable, but the lower risk profile of existing channels aligns with PE objectives
risks: Brand may be difficult to differentiate through third-party dealerships that carry multiple brands
Distributor margin and allowances compress profitability significantly ($3K vs. $10K per bike)
The European brand may face credibility challenges in the US market without a dedicated retail presence
Addressable market may be as small as ~450 bikes if European origin is a meaningful purchase driver, making even 83-bike breakeven competitive
next_steps: Conduct market research to validate size and growth of high-end sporty segment and identify key competitors
Negotiate distribution agreements and select 2-3 high-volume US dealership partners
Evaluate whether US expansion is the best use of capital vs. growing in underpenetrated European markets
Set a 12-18 month review milestone to assess whether volumes justify investing in a flagship dealership
